                 Abstract
                 As Malaysia pushes toward its national net-zero emissions goal, carbon capture and storage (CCS) is
                 emerging as a key decarbonization strategy for the oil and gas sector. Depleted hydrocarbon reservoirs, with
                 their well-understood geology and existing infrastructure, offer promising sites for permanent CO2 storage.
                 This study introduces a decision-support framework designed to optimize CO2 injection site selection
                 across Malaysian reservoirs, aiming to maximize storage potential while maintaining pressure safety and
                 reducing logistical hurdles. The framework is specifically tailored for early-stage CCS project screening
                 and planning.
                    We developed a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model to identify the best reservoirs for CO2
                 injection. Each candidate reservoir was evaluated based on storage capacity, distance to CO2 compression
                 platforms, and pressure response under injection. A simplified gas tank model estimates pressure buildup
                 from CO2 injection, with constraints to avoid exceeding fracture pressure or operational safety limits. The
                 model balances CO2 storage volume against transport costs linked to source-to-sink distance, maximizing
                 net storage utility. Additionally, we also explored and compared alternative nature-inspired optimization
                 algorithms as part of the study.
                    When applied to real-world Malaysian reservoir data, the framework revealed that pressure constraints
                 and location-based costs heavily influence injection site selection. Some high-capacity reservoirs were
                 deprioritized due to pressure risks or unfavorable distances. The MILP model allows rapid scenario testing
                 and sensitivity analysis, highlighting the need for early pressure screening to prevent costly CO2 allocation
                 mistakes in later project stages.
                    This study presents a practical optimization approach for Malaysia’s regional CCS planning, supporting
                 industry efforts to achieve net-zero targets. By integrating reservoir capacity, geographic logistics, and
                 pressure safety constraints, the framework offers a scalable and efficient alternative to traditional screening
                 methods. The inclusion of a gas-law-based pressure model at the pre-screening stage ensures realistic and
                 safe site evaluations without extensive simulations.

                 Introduction
                 Currently, PETRONAS is spearheading large-scale CCS initiatives to establish Malaysia as a regional
                 storage hub, with several candidate storage locations identified, including the Duyong, Penyu, and Lawit
                 fields offshore Peninsular Malaysia (PETRONAS 2025). While depleted hydrocarbon reservoirs offer
                 favorable characteristics such as known geology and existing infrastructure, selecting suitable storage sites
                 remains technically complex and requires careful consideration of pressure management and geomechanical
                 constraints to ensure long-term storage integrity (Mustafa et al. 2022).
                    Central to the success of such large-scale deployment is the ability to model and optimize the
                 CO2 supply chain from capture to storage. Transporting CO2 at pressures above the critical point is
                 generally advantageous because dense-phase CO2 exhibits high density, which reduces volumetric flow
                 rates and can lower pipeline diameters and compression requirements. However, operation in this regime
                 introduces important technical challenges. The thermophysical properties of CO2 near the critical region
                 are highly sensitive to pressure, temperature, and fluid composition. Small concentrations of impurities
                 such as hydrogen, nitrogen, or methane can significantly modify phase behavior, density, viscosity, and
                 compressibility, thereby affecting hydraulic performance, compression power requirements, and flow
                 assurance margins. Previous studies have shown that CO2 purity can influence pipeline design, operating
                 pressure windows, and overall transport network cost, particularly in shared infrastructure serving multiple
                 capture sources (Wetenhall et al. 2014). As a result, accounting for these sensitivities is essential when
                 evaluating dense-phase CO2 transport and storage options at an early stage.
                    Research has shown that hub-based optimization models can significantly reduce CCS infrastructure
                 costs through economies of scale and centralized transport and storage systems (Zhang et al. 2018).
                 However, many traditional optimization frameworks treat storage reservoirs as static sinks with fixed
                 capacity limits. More recent studies demonstrate that integrating physics-based reservoir dynamics,
                 including pressure evolution and injectivity constraints, directly into mixed-integer linear programming
                 (MILP) formulations provides a more realistic assessment of both transport feasibility and storage
                 performance (D’Amore and Bezzo 2021; Bertoni et al. 2025).
                    Preliminary studies using nodal analysis further highlight the value of evaluating CO2 injectivity and
                 its interaction with surface and subsurface infrastructure at an early stage of the project lifecycle (An and
                 Kwon 2025). Such early-stage assessments are particularly important given the strong thermodynamic
                 sensitivities of dense-phase CO2, which can complicate pipeline hydraulics and flow assurance. Although
                 detailed numerical simulations are typically deferred until the Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) stage,
                 previous work indicates that integral thermo-hydraulic models can provide sufficiently reliable predictions
                 of dense-phase CO2 transport for initial screening and concept selection (Martynov et al. 2015).

                 CCS Value Chain
                 The transport of CO2 molecule in a CCS chain spans hundreds of kilometers and several kilometers of
                 vertical depth. Unlike natural gas or oil, CO2 exhibits a unique sensitivity to pressure and temperature near
                 its critical point (73.8 bar and 31.1°C), making the understanding of the expected pressure and temperatures
                 profile a fundamental requirement for both design and operation.

                    Point 1: The stream at this stage is a low-density gas, highly sensitive to impurities. The presence of non-
                 condensable gases such as nitrogen and hydrogen significantly alters compression or pumping requirements.
                 These "light" components increase the work required by compressors and shift the phase envelope, often

                 a stable dense-phase transition.

                 typical in subsea environments. Target delivery pressures are commonly in the range of 100-200 bar to
                 overcome cumulative frictional losses and reservoir backpressure while maintaining an adequate margin
                 above the two-phase region. Operation in the dense phase combines gas-like viscosity with liquid-like
                 density, typically in the range of 600-900 kg/m3, enabling high mass flow rates through the pipeline and
                 into the reservoir.
                    Point 2 to 3: Along the CO2 transmission segment, the pressure profile is governed by Darcy—Weisbach
                 frictional losses and hydrostatic effects associated with seafloor bathymetry. Dense-phase transport is
                 hydraulically efficient, and large trunklines, typically 16–24 inches in diameter, may exhibit pressure drops
                 on the order of 0.1 bar per kilometer, depending on flow rate and fluid density. Subsea pipelines may
                 approach thermal equilibrium with the seabed over hundred meter-scale distances, although the rate of
                 convergence depends on insulation and operating conditions. Seabed temperatures are commonly in the
                 range of 20–30°C in tropical regions and may decrease to approximately 4°C in cold deepwater. Lower
                 temperatures increase CO2 density, reducing flow velocity for a given mass rate and lowering frictional
                 pressure losses. However, excessive pressure reduction may lead to entry into the two-phase region,
                 resulting in slug flow, mechanical vibration, and unstable wellhead conditions.
                    Point 3 to 4: The transition from pipeline to wellbore is controlled by the injection choke, which serves as
                 the primary point of active operational control. The choke dissipates excess pipeline pressure and regulates
                 the injection rate. As CO2 passes through the choke, it undergoes near-isenthalpic expansion. Because CO2
                 exhibits a relatively high Joule—Thomson coefficient under these conditions, significant throttling can lead
                 to rapid temperature reduction. Very low CO2 temperatures, below approximately –20°C, pose risks of
                 thermal shock to steel, seal embrittlement, and the formation of hydrates or solid CO2.
                    Point 4 to 5: As CO2 descends through the injection tubing, the pressure profile is dominated by the
                 hydrostatic head of the fluid column. In deep offshore wells, the weight of a dense-phase CO2 column
                 can contribute tens of bar, and in very deep wells potentially approaching hundreds of bar, to the pressure
                 available at the sandface, in some cases enabling near-passive injection. Geothermal warming during
                 descent increases fluid temperature, which reduces CO2 density and correspondingly lowers the hydrostatic
                 contribution.
                    Point 5 to 6: At the sandface, injection occurs when the flowing bottomhole pressure Pbh exceeds the
                 reservoir pressure Pr. Although the damaged zone around the wellbore, arising from drilling, fines migration,
                 or scale deposition, is physically limited in extent, it can impose substantial additional pressure loss at CCS-
                 scale injection rates. Skin represents a localized resistance that effectively consumes available sandface
                 pressure. Even moderate positive skin values can reduce injectivity by tens of percent and require additional
                 pressure on the order of tens of bar.
                    Point 6 to 7: At the formation scale, reservoir pressure evolution is governed by cumulative injected
                 mass or volume. For early-stage assessment, the P/z tank model provides a suitable representation, linking
                 cumulative injection to average reservoir pressure through a linear relationship. This temporal coupling is
                 important when optimization must balance short-term injection targets against longer-term pressure build-
                 up and storage constraints.

                 Methods
                 With the end-to-end pressure profile established, the analysis shifts to the hydraulic constraints used for
                 reservoir selection within a CCS hub. These calculations enable rapid screening of candidate sites during the
                 early project phases, by identifying injection-rate and pressure limitations that may constrain feasibility. By
                 applying hydraulic limits upfront, potential bottlenecks can be identified before undertaking more detailed
                 and capital-intensive studies. Geomechanical and geochemical effects, while critical to long-term storage
                 integrity, are beyond the scope of this work and are considered separately.

                 Overview of the modelling framework
                 A dynamic, pressure-aware optimisation framework is proposed. The framework couples:
                    1. A physics-based transport and injection model, which evaluates the cost and pressure response
                       associated with injecting CO2 into a given reservoir at its current pressure state; and
                    2. A linear optimisation layer, which allocates the required CO2 disposal rate across candidate reservoirs
                       on an annual basis.
                    The framework is designed explicitly for screening and pre-FEED analysis, where rapid scenario
                 evaluation and transparent physical interpretation are prioritised over detailed geomechanical or multiphase
                 simulation.

                 Implications for CCS planning
                 The results demonstrate that CCS network design cannot rely on static cost or distance metrics. Instead,
                 optimal reservoir selection is inherently dynamic, driven by cumulative pressure build-up and injectivity
                 limits. The results show that transporting CO2 farther to a high-quality reservoir can be economically
                 superior to forcing injection into a nearby but tight formation.

                 Limitations and Future Extensions
                 The modelling framework presented in this paper captures the dominant couplings between CO2 transport,
                 reservoir pressure build-up, and injectivity-controlled well performance. Nevertheless, several simplifying
                 assumptions were made to enable tractable optimisation, and these define clear pathways for future
                 improvement.

                 Reservoir fracture constraint
                 In the present method, storage integrity is enforced through a maximum allowable average reservoir
                 pressure, Pr ≤ Pfrac. In practice, fracture initiation is governed by the local wellbore pressure rather than
                 the average reservoir pressure. A more physically representative constraint is Pbh(t) ≤ Pfrac, where Pbh is
                 the flowing bottom-hole injection pressure computed from the radial flow equation (Eq. 5). Because Pbh
                 > Pr, the current formulation is conservative for highly injective reservoirs but may be non-conservative
                 for tighter formations, where large near-well pressure gradients can induce fracture even when the average
                 reservoir pressure remains moderate.
                    In the present case study, a single injection well is assigned to each pipeline and reservoir. This
                 configuration concentrates the total injection rate into one well, which in some cases leads to elevated
                 bottom-hole pressures (as observed in Figure 8). In realistic CCS developments, injection is typically
                 distributed across multiple wells, allowing total injectivity to be increased while maintaining acceptable
                 wellbore pressures. Incorporating multiple wells would therefore enable the constraint Pbh ≤ Pfrac to be
                 enforced more realistically.
                    A natural extension of the model would replace the tank-model fracture constraint Pr ≤ Pfrac with a
                 wellbore-based constraint of the form Pbh(Pr, m, ̇ kh) ≤ Pfrac, thereby coupling injectivity, flow allocation,
                 and fracture risk more directly.

                 Hydrostatic pressure effects
                 The present model neglects hydrostatic pressure effects along pipelines and wellbores. While may
                 acceptable for early-stage screening, hydrostatic pressure can be significant for dense-phase CO2 transport,
                 particularly in offshore CCS settings with large water depths or deep injection intervals. Future extensions
                 should incorporate hydrostatic pressure contributions to better capture elevation effects on compression
                 requirements and fracture-pressure margins.

                 Booster stations and multi-segment pipelines
                 The current model assumes a single compression stage at the capture plant and no intermediate booster
                 stations. For long pipelines, however, the economically optimal configuration often involves multiple
                 compressors to avoid excessive discharge pressure and material limits.

                 Network topology
                 Finally, the current hub-and-spoke configuration assigns one pipeline per reservoir. Future work could
                 include shared trunklines and branching networks, allowing economies of scale and network effects to be
                 captured explicitly.

                 Conclusions
                 This study demonstrates that CCS site selection cannot rely on static volumetric capacity alone. Integrating
                 physics-based hydraulic constraints into the early-stage screening process shows that transport distance
                 and reservoir pressure limits may govern the practical feasibility of a storage site more strongly than its
                 theoretical storage volume.
                    The hydraulic calculations required to evaluate dense-phase CO2 transport are computationally
                 straightforward to implement and can be applied at an early stage of project development. Deferring such
                 assessments until later project phase is therefore not strictly necessary. Incorporating these calculations
                 during initial screening allows operators to identify critical constraints related to compression requirements
                 and pipeline sizing before undertaking more detailed and resource-intensive analyses, such as transient flow
                 assurance studies.
                    The framework presented in this paper was developed within the constraints of a short-duration
                 project and is intended as an exploratory, screening-level tool. The modeling components are deliberately
                 simplified and integrated in a pragmatic manner to support rapid assessment rather than comprehensive
                 physical representation. As a result, further work is required to refine the methodology, relax simplifying
                 assumptions, and validate the results against detailed reservoir and flow simulations.
